lead: k-nearest neighbour (kNN) keeps the training examples and their labels. To classify a new query, it measures how far the query is from each stored example, picks the k closest ones, and returns the majority label. It builds no equation or tree before prediction. It is used in image search, simple recommendation, medical screening baselines and handwritten digit recognition. Its weakness is cost at prediction time and sensitivity to feature scale.
prereq: You need: Unit 1 on distance and data representation; Unit 2 on cross-validation for choosing k.

blocks.text: kNN stores a training set D = {(x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>)}. Each x<sub>i</sub> is a feature vector and y<sub>i</sub> is its class label. A query x is classified only when it arrives. No parameters are fitted before that. This is why some syllabi call kNN instance-based learning or memory-based learning.

blocks.where: d is the Euclidean distance; x<sub>j</sub> is the query's j-th feature; x<sub>ij</sub> is stored example i's j-th feature; p is the number of features.

items: For a query x, compute d(x, x<sub>i</sub>) to every stored point.
Sort the distances and keep the k smallest.
For classification, take the majority label among those k; for regression, take their mean y.
Optional: weight each neighbour by 1/d or 1/(d+ε).

blocks.text: For two classes, an odd k avoids a tie. With k = 1, every stored point owns a region: a query in that region is closer to that point than to any other. These regions are Voronoi cells.

Small k follows local detail and can fit noise. Large k smooths across many points and can wash out a small class. Choose k by cross-validation on training folds, never on the test set. A common starting point is a small odd number, then tune it.

blocks.where: ŷ is the predicted class; N<sub>k</sub>(x) is the set of k nearest stored points; c is a class label; w<sub>i</sub> is the neighbour's weight.

blocks.text: Distance-weighted kNN uses wi = 1/d(x, xi), or wi = 1/(d+ε) with a tiny ε > 0 to avoid division by zero. A close neighbour then counts more than a far one. For regression, return the weighted mean of the neighbours' y values. For a local linear fit instead of a local vote, see Chapter 3.9.

sections.h3: Scale and the shape of the boundary

blocks.text: Features carry units. A salary in rupees may range from 10,000 to 1,00,000; age ranges from 18 to 70. Squared salary differences are about 10<sup>6</sup> times larger (up to 8.1 × 10<sup>9</sup> against about 2.7 × 10<sup>3</sup>), so Euclidean distance ignores age. Standardise each feature before kNN: z = (x − μ)/σ, where μ is the training mean and σ is the training standard deviation. Use the same μ and σ for the query.

kNN is non-parametric: it does not fix a small set of coefficients. Its boundary can follow any shape, but it needs the training data at prediction time. For 1NN the plane is cut into Voronoi cells: every query in a cell is closer to that cell's stored point than to any other. In high dimensions many distances become similar; see Unit 4, principal component analysis, for reducing dimensions. A large-margin alternative is support vector machines.

figure.caption: Q(2,2) with all five stored points; the three shortest distances (B 1.00, A 1.41, D 2.24) are the k = 3 neighbours, and the longer lines to C and E are ignored. Two neighbours are positive and one is negative, so the majority vote predicts +.

spec.aria: A query point Q at (2,2) with lines to all five stored points labelled by distance; the three nearest points B, A and D are highlighted, and their labels are two positive and one negative, giving a majority vote of positive.

examples.question: Training points: A(1,1)+, B(2,1)+, C(4,4)−, D(4,3)−, E(5,4)−. Query Q(2,2), k = 3. Compute all Euclidean distances. Give the majority-vote prediction and the distance-weighted prediction with weights 1/d.
steps: Write Q = (2,2). For each point use d = √((x<sub>Q</sub>−x<sub>i</sub>)² + (y<sub>Q</sub>−y<sub>i</sub>)²).
Sorted distances: B 1.00, A 1.41, D 2.24, C 2.83, E 3.61. The three nearest are B(+), A(+), D(−).
Majority vote: + has 2 votes, − has 1 vote, so predict +.
examples.answer: Prediction is + under both majority vote and distance-weighted vote.
examples.check:
import math
pts = [('A',1,1,'+'), ('B',2,1,'+'), ('C',4,4,'-'), ('D',4,3,'-'), ('E',5,4,'-')]
qx, qy = 2, 2
dist = {}
for n, x, y, lab in pts:
    dist[n] = math.hypot(qx - x, qy - y)
for n in ['B','A','D','C','E']:
    print(round(dist[n], 2))
wB = 1 / dist['B']
wA = 1 / dist['A']
wD = 1 / dist['D']
print(round(wB, 3))
print(round(wA, 3))
print(round(wD, 3))
pos = wB + wA
neg = wD
print(round(pos, 3))
print(round(neg, 3))

traps: Forgetting to scale: a feature with a large range dominates Euclidean distance. Standardise with training-set μ and σ, then use the same values on the query.
k = 1 memorises noise and overfits; a very large k smooths across classes and underfits. Tune k by cross-validation.
Tuning k on the test set leaks information. Choose k on training or validation folds, then report one final test score.
An even k can tie in a two-class problem. Use an odd k or state a tie-break rule. Weighted votes can also tie.
A zero distance makes 1/d undefined. Use 1/(d+ε) with a tiny positive ε, or give an exact match a special rule.

quiz.q: What does kNN store during training?
quiz.a: It stores the training examples and their labels, D = {(x<sub>i</sub>, y<sub>i</sub>)}. It does not fit a compact model before prediction.

quiz.q: Why is an odd k preferred for a two-class problem?
quiz.a: With an odd k, two classes cannot split the k votes equally, so a simple majority always exists. An even k can produce a tie.

quiz.q: What is the Voronoi diagram of a 1-nearest-neighbour classifier?
quiz.a: It divides the feature space into cells, one per stored point. Every query inside a cell is closer to that cell's stored point than to any other stored point, so 1NN predicts that point's label.

quiz.q: Stored points: A(0,0)+, B(1,0)+, C(0,1)−, D(3,3)−. Query Q(1,1), k = 3. Compute the Euclidean distances, list the three nearest neighbours, and give the majority vote.
quiz.a: B: d = 1.00. C: d = 1.00. A: d = 1.41. D: d = 2.83. Three nearest are B(+), C(−), A(+). Positive gets 2 votes and negative gets 1, so predict +.

quiz.q: A distance-weighted kNN has three neighbours with distances 0.5, 1.0 and 2.0 and labels +, − and −. Use weights 1/d and give the weighted vote.
quiz.a: Positive weight = 1/0.5 = 2.0. Negative weight = 1/1.0 + 1/2.0 = 1.0 + 0.5 = 1.5. Positive total 2.0 is larger, so predict +.

quiz.q: Explain the bias-variance behaviour of kNN as k goes from 1 to a very large value.
quiz.a: Small k gives low bias and high variance: the boundary follows individual points, including noise. Large k gives high bias and low variance: many distant points are averaged, so real local structure is lost. Choose k to balance the two.

quiz.q: Why is choosing k on the test set a mistake?
quiz.a: The test set must estimate performance on unseen data. If k is chosen by looking at test results, the test set has influenced the model, so the reported score is optimistic. Use cross-validation on training data to choose k, then test once.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, kNN appears in vector search for similar images and documents, in anomaly detection, and as a baseline in credit or fraud screening. Modern libraries use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes such as trees and hashing to avoid scanning every stored point. Research studies distance metrics, learned embeddings, and fairness when neighbours come from skewed data. Newer curricula often connect kNN to contrastive learning and retrieval-augmented models. Search next for approximate nearest neighbour, locality-sensitive hashing, and metric learning.
